changes.before: With supplied people and clubs, create membership with the two required foreign keys and composite key. Insert the three worked relationships; leave both parent tables unchanged.
changes.after: Store one row for each person-and-club connection.

before: A person can join several clubs, and a club can contain several people. Store each person and club once. A junction table stores one row for each relationship instead of a comma-separated list inside one cell.

membership has two required IDs. Each REFERENCES clause points to a parent primary key; the composite key forbids the same relationship twice. PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON enables enforcement on this SQLite connection before writes. The two JOIN operations follow the stored IDs to readable names; aliases p, c and m name each role. The project checks successful rows; the local error example below separately demonstrates the rejected write.
Optional practice: add a new club parent, then connect one existing person to its ID. Explain why an unknown club ID is not a valid relationship.
after: One person can join several clubs, and one club can have several people. A junction table stores these connections: one row for each person-and-club pair.
Require both IDs and make the pair a primary key. Foreign keys make each ID point to an existing parent row. Turn on SQLite's foreign-key checks before adding the relationships.
If Oren joins Music, add the pair `(2, 20)` to membership. Oren and Music already exist, so neither parent table needs another copy.
The project supplies people and clubs. Create only the membership table, enable foreign-key checks, and store `(1, 10)`, `(1, 20)`, and `(2, 10)`. Keep both parent tables unchanged.
A relationship pointing to club 99 fails because that club does not exist. Missing IDs and repeated pairs also break the declared rules. Keep intentional failures out of the normal project run.

project.title: Connect many people to many clubs
project.task: Using the supplied people and clubs, create membership with required foreign keys and a primary key using both IDs. Insert (1,10), (1,20), and (2,10).
